teaching.task: # HMS Year 11 V11 (The body and mind in motion): nutrition for the energy systems. How does what an athlete eats decide which energy system can actually keep running? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Nutrition is the supply chain for those fuels. You met the three macronutrients in digestion: carbohydrate in a small glycogen store, fat in a huge store, and protein for building and repair. What's new is which system each one feeds. Carbohydrate is the only food fuel the body can use without oxygen, so it feeds glycolysis and the aerobic system. Fat feeds only the aerobic system. And protein has no fuel store, so it adds only a small share of exercise energy. From last time, intensity decides the mix. At rest, fat supplies most of the energy. At about sixty-five per cent of maximum effort, the two are roughly equal. That's the crossover. Above about eighty-five per cent of maximum effort, carbohydrate supplies most of it. Now the puzzle. The runner spends long stretches above the crossover, so most of their energy comes from a store that lasts about ninety minutes. Carbohydrate decides whether they finish the session. The shot putter's efforts last seconds, run on phosphocreatine, and cost little in total. Their priority is protein, to build muscle. So the same meals can't suit both, and it's the runner who's short-changed. So how much does an active person need? Guidelines are written per kilogram of body mass per day, because a bigger body needs more of the same things. And carbohydrate tracks training load: about three to five grams per kilogram for light training, and six to ten for heavy endurance work. Take a sixty-kilogram netballer in light training. Three to five, times sixty, is one hundred and eighty to three hundred grams. A ninety-five-kilogram rower in heavy training: six to ten, times ninety-five, is five hundred and seventy to nine hundred and fifty grams. On the same diet, the netballer is covered, and the rower gets about a third of what they need.

scenes.teachingReason: So how much does an active person need? Guidelines are written per kilogram of body mass per day, because a bigger body needs more of the same things. On the same diet, the netballer is covered, and the rower gets about a third of what they need.

scenes.teachingReason: Protein rises from about one point two grams per kilogram to about two in heavy training. But two is roughly a ceiling. Beyond it, the extra isn't stored as muscle. It's burned, or stored as fat. The training is the signal to grow, and protein is the material. Fat works the other way. It has a floor, about twenty to thirty-five per cent of energy, and rarely below twenty. Too little, and the body can't absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, or make some hormones well. Very low intakes can also lead to low energy availability, which you met earlier.

scenes.teachingReason: Now the iron puzzle. Micronutrients, the vitamins and minerals we need in tiny amounts, carry no energy. They're part of the machinery that releases it. Iron sits at the centre of haemoglobin, and of myoglobin in muscle. It's what oxygen binds to. Without enough iron, less oxygen reaches the mitochondria, so the aerobic system is capped lower. At the same pace, more energy has to come from the anaerobic systems, and fatigue comes sooner. So iron doesn't give energy. It removes a limit. But only if you're short of it. Extra iron gives a well-stocked athlete nothing, and too much does harm. A blood test decides, not a label.

scenes.teachingReason: Last, water. It has no energy, but running short hurts performance fastest. As you saw with the delivery chain, sweat shrinks the plasma, so stroke volume falls, heart rate climbs, and less blood reaches the skin, so core temperature rises. In team sport, a skill error can be an early sign. What to drink, and when, comes later.
